A Principal Reflects on Shame and School Bullying

Daniel Frank Ph.D.

Daniel Frank

Daniel Frank   Daniel B. Frank, Ph.D. is the Principle of the Francis W. Parker School in Chicago and Executive Editor of the education journal Schools: Studies in Education, published by the University of Chicago Press.

It is the business of the school environment to eliminate, so far as possible, the unworthy features of the existing social environment from influence upon mental habitudes. It establishes a purified medium of action. Selection aims not only at simplifying but at weeding out what is undesirable. Every society gets encumbered with what is trivial, with dead wood from the past and with what is positively perverse. The school has the duty of omitting such things from the environment which it supplies, and thereby doing what it can do to counteract their influence in the ordinary social environment. [John Dewey, 1916/1944, p. 20]

“We may not be able to stop all the evil in the world, but I know that how we treat one another is entirely up to us.” [A high school student]

A SYSTEMS PSYCHODYNAMIC PERSPECTIVE

Educators in schools are always trying to balance the needs of the individual with the needs of the group. Creating a profound sense of community as a foundation for students to learn about the world and learn about themselves is an essential goal of any good education. Understanding the tensions between the sometimes conflicting and sometimes complimentary needs of the person and the public, the self and society calls on school leaders and classroom teachers to appreciate how culture influences individual behavior and how individual behavior, in turn, influences culture.

When problems arise in schools, and they inevitably do, it is important for leaders to be able to understand and have the analytic, social, and psychological skills to address the loving and hateful feelings people bring with them into school each day. A worldview that can take into account the relationship between the broader dynamics of social systems and structures and the feelings and meanings that are evoked in the people who are living in relationship to those specific systems and structures, can provide a lifeline of support for vital institutional strategic thinking and action. This worldview is informed by understandings about human experience drawn from the fields of social systems and psychoanalysis.

Alan Sugarman Ph.D.

Alan Sugarman

Alan Sugarman   Alan Sugarman, Ph.D. is a Training and Supervising Psychoanalyst and Supervising Child and Adolescent Psychoanalyst, San Diego Psychoanalytic Society and Institute; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of California, San Diego

Freud's (1919) classic paper, “A Child Is Being Beaten,” with its introduction to masochism, offers an excellent example of how child psychoanalytic data can clarify his ideas, correct those where he went astray, and check whether ones that seem speculative are supported by developmental data. Toward these ends, the analysis of a three-year-old girl with prominent beating fantasies is presented. Her analytic material suggests that it is unimportant from a treatment or pathogenesis perspective to differentiate between different types of sadomasochistic content in such fantasies. That is, the phenomenological distinction between beating fantasies and beating wishes does not seem to have much practical utility. All such fantasies have the same essential structure and are compromise formations in which pain is sought to maintain the complex equilibrium provided by them. Her material also indicates that such phenomena do not require oedipal stage engagement or dynamics to develop, although they will, of course, be colored by this stage's issues as the child engages it. Even sexualization, the so-called hallmark of beating fantasies, can arise as a means to deal with various cumulative traumas and does not require access to the sexual stirrings of the oedipal stage to occur.

I focus this presentation on the patient–analyst relationship within the frame of contemporary psychoanalysis. To do so, I take the Freudian origins of transference as a starting point, then move on to the evolution of the concept of countertransference, and finally reach the essential point: the theory of the analytical field, such as it was described by Willy and Madeleine Baranger, including my own perspective of the subject.

The authors work with ideas about structures and how those structures constitute individual actors. Coercion in Groups: Finding One's Voice; Knowing One's Mind

Marilyn Charles ABPP

Marilyn Charles

Marilyn Charles   Marilyn Charles, Ph.D., ABPP is at the Austen Riggs Center. This article is an expanded version of a paper being presented at the 2008 meeting of the American Psychological Association, Boston, MA.

Groups develop standards to facilitate their function and yet the standards that evolve are not always in line with the explicit task of the group. Group pressures and anxieties can move towards relief of strain in ways that may actually oppose the group's intended goals. The larger the group, the more difficult it may be to catch hold of relatively invisible coercive forces that guide behaviour. As Bion (1977) notes, group pressures tend to move towards cohesion and tradition, and away from the new idea that ultimately might be productive but would also be disregulating. Although clinicians learn about tensions between the individual and the group from a theoretical perspective, engaging with these tensions actively and reflectively can enhance both our understanding and our practice, as we discover ways in which we are buffeted by and at times succumb to these same processes. As a way of considering some of the more subtle ways in which we may find ourselves behaving out of line with our own integrity in relation to encounters with implicit group demands, I will use some of my own experiences in a group setting to highlight and illustrate some of these coercive forces that may work against the integration of new ideas in group settings.

Marilyn Nissim-Sabat

Marilyn Nissim-Sabat   Marilyn Nissim-Sabat, Ph.D., M.S.W. is Professor Emeritus, Department of Philosophy, Lewis University. She is a psychotherapist in private practice in Chicago.

Historically, psychoanalysis has failed to differentiate adequately between aggression and assertion. It is uncontroversial to state that bullying is a form of aggression. However, if aggression and assertion are not adequately distinguished, bullying could also be viewed as a form of assertion. Some psychoanalysts have attempted to resolve this by using the terms aggression and assertion as synonyms but introducing the notion of nondestructive aggression. Bullying, then, is understood to be hostile aggression or hostile assertion. In this article, I aim to prepare psychoanalytic and philosophical groundwork for a meaningful differentiation between aggression and assertion, and, at the same time, to shed light on the nature of bullying, parental bullying in particular. To achieve these aims, I critique an aspect of the case material presented by Frank Summers in his (2005) book, Self Creation: Psychoanalytic Therapy and the Art of the Possible. I also critique Parens' (2008) notion of nondestructive aggression as used by him and by Summers. Additionally, I discuss some of the philosophical notions Summers introduces and discusses relevant to a critique of his notion of the analyst's vision of the patient's development in its relevance to his case of Anna.

Adele Kaufman

Adele Kaufman   Adele Kaufman is a Training and Supervising Analyst; Children and Adolescent Supervising Analyst; Chair, Child and Adolescent Analysis Committee, Chicago Institute For Psychoanalysis.

The purpose of this clinical article is to discuss aspects of the analysis of a child whose adoption functioned as organizer of her personality. Her fantasy life, defensive organization, sense of self and other, and object relations were all organized around a personal mythology surrounding her adoption. These organizing myths took various forms that emerged in the course of the analysis. Her adoptive parents also created a mythology that had a critical impact on the child's development and on their development as parents. The analytic work demonstrates how these organizing mythologies governed the parent–child relationship and how the collision of their mythologies led to a breakdown in the child's development and in parental functioning. In the course of the analysis, the child developed the capacity to grieve and to react to loss in an organized way as progressive development was restored and she was able to feel valued and loved. Her parents began to grieve the dual loss of not having biological children or a perfect adoption, and to develop more motherly and fatherly feelings for their child.

Sonia is a case study of a little girl who presented at age 2 years, 10 months for temper tantrums that drove her parents crazy. Gradually, her doll play revealed a preoccupation with the genital difference and explicit references to her “lost penis,” accompanied by frank urogenital sensations. This play, as well as bedtime anxiety, led to our understanding the extent to which she was absorbed in symptomatic masturbatory behavior that, in turn, was interfering with her development and spoke to the need for more intensive treatment. In the course of her ensuing analysis, which began at age 4, we uncovered the multiple meanings and secondary gains embedded in her masturbatory behavior and accompanying fantasies. Furthermore, over time, we uncovered evidence of a learning difference that had contributed substantially both to her sense of defectiveness and to her ability to master learning about her body and about her affects.

Denia Barrett MSW

Denia Barrett

Denia Barrett   Denia G. Barrett is a graduate of the Hanna Perkins Center Child Therapy Course, Cleveland, Ohio. She is a child and adolescent psychoanalyst in private practice in Chicago, IL.

Sonia was not yet three when she and her parents began their work with Dr. Sherkow, but already they were all feeling quite distraught and desperate for help, especially with bedtime struggles that drove the parents crazy. Sonia conveyed her concrete understanding of their complaint and her own parallel state of distress through her play. In one story she was perpetually “driven crazy” by a bus or taxi driver who frustrated her efforts to “get somewhere.” Dr. Sherkow got a strong taste of the crazy feeling when assigned the role of the driver commanded to go from one wrong destination to another, or of the baby who was “kept in a constant state of yearning.” Dr. Sherkow has organized her case presentation around the vicissitudes of Sonia's masturbation fantasies, although she likens this approach to looking solely at one artist's contributions to a whole school of painting and leaving aside those of others. One feels that she could not have written her chapter in any other way, as Sonia's compulsive masturbation at home and in her analytic sessions demands that one pay attention to its intrusion on all aspects of her functioning. Winnicott (1975), in his paper identifying the role of the depressive position in normal emotional development, comments to analysts who suggest that an infant may reach that achievement in the first half of the first year: “What a pity to spoil a valuable concept by making it difficult to believe in” (p. 263). In reading this case, I found myself wanting to say something along the same lines to Sonia: “What a pity to spoil a valuable pleasure by making it difficult to get relief from.” Freud (1905) considered masturbation to represent “the executive agency of the whole of infantile sexuality” (footnote, p. 189) and he recognized the organizing function it serves for development and the integration of body, mind, and object world. Sonia, however, turns too much to her body to rid herself of a tormenting sense of loss and yearning that is driving her mad. Driving each other crazy seems to be how she and her parents have found to organize how they relate to one another, but the good news is that they want help to escape this pattern.

Scott Boles Ph.D.

Scott Boles

Scott Boles   Scott A. Boles, Ph.D. is an instructor in the Child, Adolescent, and Adult Training Programs in Psychoanalysis at the San Diego Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, and a Consultant to the Hanna Fenichel Center for Child Development.

This article summarizes the treatment of a severely disturbed four-year-old boy who represents the widening scope of child analysis—a boy whose exposure to an array of traumas undermined his ego development, distorted his object relations, and interfered with his developmental progression. Earlier generations of analysts would have viewed such a child as possessing too many ego deviations or deficits to be considered analyzable. Such traditional ideas about analyzability are at odds with more recent research, however. Thus, Fonagy's and Target's (1996) research found child analysis to be the optimal treatment for children with severe and complex psychopathology. This article presents analytic material that supports this research and demonstrates (1) that severely disturbed children are analyzable and capable of deep and meaningful change, (2) that early intervention is imperative, (3) that an analytic framework involving four or more sessions per week is essential in containing and regulating affect, (4) how functioning as a developmental object helps build the necessary mental structures to experience conflict, (5) that serving as a developmental object does not have to preclude the development of transference or a psychoanalytic process, and (6) that the analyst's gender can play an important role in promoting development and facilitating treatment.

Prologue: Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Bullying

Christine Kieffer

Christine Kieffer

Christine Kieffer  

The articles collected for this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry comprise a broad range of theoretical, clinical, socio-cultural, and philosophical reflections on the topic of bullying or—perhaps more broadly—psychoanalytic perspectives on the construction of power relations and their impact upon individual development and group-level functioning. The authors examine the vicissitudes of interpersonal relationships, as well as their influence upon the broader social fabric. Readers will note that many of the articles in this issue bring into the foreground the impact of a large group influences upon the construction of dyadic relationships and also highlight the embeddedness or intersubjectively constructed aspects of what has been classically thought of as a monadic mind within a more encompassing group mind. Thus, most of the articles in this article reflect, at least to some degree, an integration of a relational perspective on the mind, with its emphasis on multiple selves and the socio-cultural imbrication of psychological functioning. It is this coconstructed group- level sensibility that is often missing from accounts of bullying in newspapers, and in the commentaries of various pundits who meditate upon its sometimes tragic consequences. That is, the contributors to this issue tend to focus upon the relational interplay among roles and influences, rather than upon inflexible roles and motivations of the bully or the victim. More recently, this pairing has been expanded to include a participating audience of bystanders, who more accurately serve as much more than an audience or Greek chorus but, rather, as active coconstructors of events.

Stuart W. Twemlow and Frank C. Sacco, psychoanalysts who are justly famous for their work in community psychiatry, introduce our topic by delineating a number of “universal truths,” many of which concern the broader, more hidden processes of the group mind. Twemlow and Sacco first point out that bullying is an inevitable aspect of interpersonal relations, as individuals or groups strive to influence others, and push for the hegemony of their desires and ideals. Twemlow and Sacco then bring into the foreground subtly disguised influences of bystanders in promoting bullying dynamics, giving these dynamics a more nuanced expression, as well as greater force.
